ann_116.text: Through this part, capital gains from 0 to 6849 US dollars clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 8%.
The drop is clearly even larger for people born in Iran: from about 68% to about 3%, against about 62% to about 8% for everyone else.
Being born in Iran by itself raises it to about 68% through this part (on the training data only).

ann_117.text: This part acts only on the 26 people born in Thailand, and 21 of them have an income of $50,000 or less.

For the typical person it acts on (a 37-year-old Asian or Pacific Islander married man born in Thailand, a high-school graduate in other service work in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it clearly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 85% to about 94%.
For the typical person overall, being born in Thailand clearly raises it through this part from about 62% to about 83%.

ann_118.text: This part acts on the 15748 husbands among 39073 training people, and 8658 of them have an income of $50,000 or less.

For the typical person it acts on (a 43-year-old White husband born in the United States, a high-school graduate in craft or repair work in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it slightly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 61% to about 63%.
Through it, not being a husband slightly lowers it for the typical person, from about 62% to about 60%.

ann_119.text: This part acts on the 4853 executives and managers among 39073 training people, and 2531 of them have an income of $50,000 or less.

For the typical person it acts on (a 41-year-old White married man born in the United States with a bachelor's degree, an executive or manager in the private sector working 40 hours a week), it clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 45% to about 28%.
For the typical person overall, an executive or managerial job clearly lowers it through this part from about 62% to about 43%.

ann_120.text: This part acts only on the 12 people in the armed forces, and 9 of them have an income of $50,000 or less.

For the typical person it acts on (a 26-year-old White never-married man born in the United States, not living in a family, a high-school graduate in the armed forces working for the federal government 40 hours a week), it slightly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 93% to about 96% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
For the typical person overall, serving in the armed forces raises it through this part from about 62% to about 73% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).

ann_121.text: Switching this part off makes almost no difference to the predictions.

ann_122.text: Through this part, being born in Italy slightly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 62% to about 64% (on the training data only).
Switching this part off makes almost no difference to the predictions.

ann_123.text: Across the whole model, a higher education level (7 to 13 on the 1-16 scale), capital gains (0 to 6849 US dollars) and capital losses (0 to 1887 US dollars) clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 86% to about 30%, from about 62% to about 8% and from about 62% to about 31%.

Being never married clearly raises it to about 99% and other ways of not being married to about 98%, being a woman to about 84%, other service work or farming or fishing to about 87% and handling or cleaning work to about 81%.

Being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers it to about 25%, not living in a family to about 35% and being unmarried to about 40%; being older (22 to 58 years) lowers it from about 73% to about 46% and longer hours (24 to 55 a week) from about 74% to about 50%, all clearly.
Preschool as the highest education raises it to above 99%, while 1st-4th or 5th-6th grade lowers it to about 19% and a master's degree raises it to about 73% (on the training data only).

Being born in Guatemala, the Dominican Republic or Colombia raises it to above 99%, and in Yugoslavia lowers it to about 32%; a missing work class raises it to about 82% and federal government work lowers it to about 49% (on the training data only).
Never having worked raises it to above 99% and being born in Laos to about 89% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this: only 9 and 17 people).

ann_116.original: Hypothesis (supported): the full capital-gain contribution to the logit of P(income<=50K) (identity node cg_term collects the direct edge, relay 194 and hinges 1266/8342). It is a concave, monotonically decreasing piecewise-linear function of standardized capital-gain: slope -1.62 up to x=0.359 (~3.8k USD), -3.76 up to x=0.496 (~4.8k USD), then -5.83, because ReLU 1266 = relu(0.976x-0.35) and 8342 = relu(0.893*1266-0.12) switch on in sequence and both carry negative output weights. Relay 194 = relu(1.24x - 0.485 nc20 + 0.867) is always active except for native-country:20 (Iran, 50 train rows), where it is zeroed, giving those rows a steeper linear slope (-3.11) and +0.25 logit at zero gain. Evidence (train, n=39073): term = +1.30 at zero gain (91% of rows), -0.19 at x=0.52, -7.2 at x=1.73, -74 at the 99999 cap; logit-term SD 5.54 (largest single term). Mean-ablating it drops train accuracy 0.852->0.824 and AUC 0.907->0.888 (3571 predictions flip). Interpretation: any sizeable capital gain is strong, increasingly steep evidence of income >50K. Closed-form (3 s.f.) max err 0.070.
ann_116.proposed: This part clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less as capital gains rise, from about 62% to about 8% at 6849 US dollars, and even more so for people born in Iran.

ann_121.original: Hypothesis (supported, functionally inert): node 3996 adds up affine relays of six one-hot inputs: 3996 = relu(1.24 nc6 + 0.942 wc1 + 0.943*15610 + 0.916*2322 + 0.912*9651 + 0.30), where 9651/2447 are always-active affine relays of workclass:5 (Self-emp-inc, inferred), 3479->16792 are exact indicators of occupation:3 (Craft-repair, inferred) that feed 2322 together with occupation:3 and native-country:41, and 15610 is a workclass:1 relay that switches off only for occupation:2 rows. On train it takes 13 distinct values in [0.46, 32.3] and is always positive. Its only consumer is node 594 in native_country22_switch, which outputs >=13 whenever native-country:22 is set and 0 otherwise regardless of 3996 (3996 would need to exceed ~99). So the whole 7-node subtree is masked: setting 3996 to 0 or to its train maximum changes the network output by exactly 0 on all 39073 train rows. It is evolutionary residue with no effect on the predictions; I found no meaningful named function for it beyond 'workclass/occupation/country one-hot score'.
ann_121.proposed: This part makes almost no difference to the predictions when switched off.

ann_122.original: Hypothesis (supported): serial composition H(nc22, A) with A = workclass_occupation_aggregator. 594 = relu(0.953 nc22 - 0.175 A - 1.07) and 1083 = relu(2.05 - 1.24*594). The standardized native-country:22 one-hot (Italy, inferred) is 21.05 when set, so 594 is between 17.0 and 18.9 for the 88 set rows and 0 otherwise; 1083 is therefore an exact NOT-indicator: 2.053 for everyone except native-country:22 rows, where it is 0. With output weight -0.024 this is a constant -0.049 logit offset that is lifted for Italy-born rows (added to the direct native-country:22 weight -0.026*21.05 = -0.55). A enters only inside the clipped region and has no effect. Evidence (train, n=39073): 1083==0 iff native-country:22 holds on every row; replacing 1083 by its constant changes P by at most 0.012 and flips 2 predictions. A negligible country bump built from a needlessly deep chain.
ann_122.proposed: This part slightly raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less for people born in Italy (on the training data only), and switching it off makes almost no difference to the predictions.

ann_123.original:
Hypothesis (supported): additive composition. Output = P(income<=50K) = sigmoid(z) (class 1 is '<=50k'). z = 1.653 + a sparse linear score over 44 directly connected standardized inputs + capital_gain_term + five one-hot indicator terms (native_country37_gate x0.030, relationship0_indicator x0.205, occupation4_indicator x-0.459, occupation2_gate x0.0086, native_country22_switch x-0.024). 57 of the 107 inputs (e.g. most native-country and several education/occupation one-hots) have no edges and are listed here as zero-effect entries; native-country:15 has a direct edge but is constant on train, so it is also inert.
Mechanism: the network is essentially logistic regression plus one nonlinear feature, a concave piecewise-linear capital-gain penalty. The direct linear part lowers P(<=50K) for married-civ-spouse (-3.38 logit when set), wives (-1.51), males (-1.18), not-in-family (-1.02), each SD of education-num (-1.15), age (-0.44), hours-per-week (-0.41) and capital-loss (-0.28); it raises it for other-service (+1.10) and farming-fishing (+1.05) occupations. Counter-intuitively, education:3/4 (1st-4th, 5th-6th grade; n=189, 406) lower P(<=50K) by ~2.0 logit when set, which partly cancels the education-num slope for these rows; I cannot give a substantive reason for this. Very rare one-hots (workclass Never-worked n=9, two native countries n=72-82, Preschool n=64) have standardized values of 20-66, so their small weights become +25 to +61 logit 'saturators' that force a <=50K prediction. Category names are inferred from PMLB's alphabetical coding.
Evidence (train, n=39073): acc 0.852, AUC 0.907, logit SD 7.25. Term SDs: capital_gain_term 5.54, direct linear 4.16, occupation4 0.26, others <0.05. Mean-ablation: capital_gain_term acc 0.852->0.824, AUC 0.907->0.888 (3571 flips); occupation4 777 flips, AUC ->0.905; relationship0 181 flips with no accuracy loss; the three rare-country/occupation gates flip <=6 predictions; the 7-node workclass_occupation_aggregator inside native_country22_switch is masked (output change exactly 0). ann_123.proposed: The whole model adds up separate effects: a higher education level, capital gains, capital losses, older age and longer hours clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, being never married or a woman clearly raises it, and being a wife clearly lowers it.

Capital gains of 6849 US dollars rather than none clearly lower it to about 8%, and even more so for people born in Iran (from about 68% to about 3%).
Being never married rather than married clearly raises it to about 99%, while being a wife rather than a husband clearly lowers it to about 25%.

The census sampling weight also lowers it, from about 65% to about 59% (on the training data only).
